Back to updates Water Column Sonar Data Collection By Data.gov admins · June 09, 2014 NOAA collects and uses active acoustic (or sonar) data for a variety of mapping requirements. As the national archive for multibeam bathymetric data, NGDC manages over 15 million nautical miles of ship trackline data from sources worldwide. In 2011, NGDC, in partnership with NOAA’s National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), initiated a new archive for high resolution data collected with sonars capable of mapping the water column. Water column sonar data are collected on NOAA fishery survey vessels and academic and international fleets, and are used to assess the physical and biological characteristics of the ocean. Primary uses include 3-D mapping of fish schools and other mid-water marine organisms, assessing biological abundance, species identification, and habitat characterization. pages.text: Wayne Rooney: Ex-Manchester United captain considered taking own life during playing career - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Rooney scored 53 goals in 120 appearances for England By Mandeep Sanghera BBC Sport journalist Published 4 hours ago Warning: This article contains references to suicide Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up". The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances. But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast , external , detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby. "When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life. "This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise." The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it". "I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added. "I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well. "I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. We Can Do Better if We Think ‘Circular.’ April 19, 2023 By: Nehika Mathur Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email Credit: nostal6ie/Shutterstock Each year, scientists calculate the date at which humanity’s demands for the Earth’s resources exceed the Earth’s capacity to regenerate what we need in a year. It’s called Earth Overshoot Day . In 1971, it fell on Dec. 25. Disturbingly, by 2022, it fell on July 28. In short, we humans need 1.75 Earths to support our current rate of consumption! That is unsustainable, and we have to make changes. So, how can we slow down our current consumption rate, while ensuring equitable progress and resources for all? Think about the products you use every day. They are created, manufactured, used and thrown away. This is often called the “take, make, use, dispose” economy. Coastal areas typically have mild weather, while the interior has greater seasonal variation in temperature and precipitation. In Nome, yearly precipitation averages about 15 inches, and the average temperature is about 21 o F. Summers average around 50 o F. Photograph: Fadel Senna/AFP/Getty Images Weather tracker Environment This article is more than 7 months old Analysis Weather tracker: Thunderstorms drench UAE and Saudi Arabia This article is more than 7 months old James Michelin for MetDesk Abnormally strong jet stream triggers deluge in Middle East, while north Africa braces for 60-80mph gusts Mon 30 Mar 2026 10.31 BST Last modified on Tue 31 Mar 2026 05.09 BST Share An unusual weather pattern unleashed severe thunderstorms across parts of the Middle East last week, battering countries including the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. The Arabian peninsula – typically dominated by arid desert climates – received up to 150mm of rain in just a few days. The deluge was caused by an abnormally strong jet stream, which helped a deep area of low pressure to develop north of Saudi Arabia . pages.text: Welcome Baseball Fans! | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Welcome Baseball Fans! If you're a fan of baseball and disability employment, you've come to the right place! At the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP), we work to increase success for people with disabilities in America's workplaces. This is a goal we share with our Alliance partner the Professional Baseball Athletic Trainers Society (PBATS). Over the years, ODEP and PBATS have collaborated on a number of activities, including the production of several public service announcements (PSAs) featuring former MLB players with disabilities and/or professional baseball athletic trainers from clubs around the country. Among the topics these PSAs address is the importance of helping people stay at or return to work after injury or illness and, most recently, strategies for fostering mental health-friendly workplaces. Please view and share these PSAs and explore our resources for fostering supportive workplaces, for all workers in all types of workplaces—because everyone should be in the game. pages.description: Discover the origin story for an accessory being comfortably lugged by nearly every hiker and student, with about 450 million sold each year
pages.text: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via public domain Humans have been carting things on our backs in wraps of some kind at least since we began using tools, around two million years ago—and we have always sought ways to make the load more comfortable. The oldest known backpack ever discovered, in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy, employed two narrow wooden boards and a hazel rod for a frame. The contraption dates to around 3300 B.C. and is credited to Ötzi the Iceman , a glacier mummy unearthed alongside it in 1991. But what we recognize as a backpack is much newer. In 1865, Henry Clay Merriam led a regiment of Black Union troops in an attack against Fort Blakely, a Confederate stronghold in Alabama. His deeds in this final battle of the Civil War earned him a Medal of Honor “for conspicuous gallantry.” Afterward, the lieutenant colonel had an epiphany: It was burdensome to carry both a knapsack (a pack with shoulder straps but no frame for internal support) and a haversack (a shoulder bag containing his rations). Based on his time carrying gear for the Army, Merriam devised a solution: a boxy canvas pack with room for socks, a quart of water, a shaving kit and a deck of cards, plus a compartment for rations in a case at the bottom. Key takeaways A college credit is a unit that measures how much time you should spend on learning activities at colleges and universities in the United States. Bachelor's degrees typically require about 120 college credits, while associate degrees usually require around 60 credits. A credit hour usually represents about one hour in class and two hours of work outside class each week, which helps determine how much time a course requires. You can earn credits in different ways to help shorten the time it takes to graduate. Learn how college credits are measured and ways you may be able to expedite earning your degree. What are college credits? A college credit is a unit that measures the amount of coursework you complete at a college or university. College credits are an important part of accreditation , or the certification that a US college or university receives when it provides a quality education [ 1 ]. Credit hours help clarify what kind of education you earn, making it easier in some cases to transfer credits from one accredited institution to another and to set a minimum standard for financial aid . Credit: wing-wing/Shutterstock A day, as we all know, is 24 hours, also known as 1,440 minutes or 86,400 seconds. Or if you’re an atomic clock maker, exactly 794,243,384,928,000 cycles of microwave radiation tuned to the ticking rate of the cesium atom . Regardless, a day is a day, right? Actually, no: An Earth day isn’t a fixed interval of time. You may have noticed news stories reporting that Earth has shaved a millisecond (thousandth of a second) or more off the time it takes to make a full rotation, or conversely, that the planet’s rotation has slowed down slightly. While some of these stories exaggerate the impacts of these changes, their basic premise is correct: Earth’s seemingly steady rotation can, at times, seem as fickle as the weather. This wouldn’t be a problem — or even noticeable — except that we have two different ways of telling time that don’t quite agree with each other. The one that probably feels most intuitive is solar time, in which a day is defined by the time it takes our planet Earth to rotate once on its axis with respect to the Sun. Jimmy Carter once gave a televised “fireside chat” while sitting by an actual White House fireplace. Questions and Answers: Problem Reporting In this section The Food and Drug Administration welcomes reports from consumers alerting the agency to problems with products regulated by FDA. These reports help FDA ensure that products on the market are safe and properly manufactured, labeled and stored. Every report is important to FDA. In each case, the information the consumer furnishes is evaluated to determine how serious the problem is and what follow-up is needed. When reviewing the information from these reports, FDA considers these factors: Is an illness or injury involved? If so, what is the health hazard? Is the illness possibly an allergic reaction--to a food or a drug (such as penicillin)--or, in the case of drugs, is it a reaction already known to occur with that product? Is the problem life-threatening? Is the product likely to be associated with the problem? Is the problem likely to be widespread or is this an isolated case? Is more information needed about the problem or the product? Is the product or problem within the jurisdiction of FDA or is it the responsibility of another federal agency or local or state government?
